newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian merger kicks off German bank revamp.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian merger kicks off German bank revamp.

text.p: A new, more vigorous phase of consolidation may be looming in German banking after two banking giants on Monday kicked off the process with a merger plan that will radically reshape the whole industry.

Analysts gave a broad thumbs-up to plans by Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel Bank AG to fuse into a Munich-centred colossus that will topple Frankfurt's Dresdner Bank AG from its number-two ranking.

Despite some risks and weaknesses related to the merger -- and some analysts voiced doubt over several strategic issues -- the move marks a major and unexpected step in an industry awash with speculation about takeovers and mergers for nearly a year.
"This is the first major merger in the German commercial banking sector," said Commerzbank AG analyst Dieter Hein, who is strongly bullish for bank shares.
"I think what we have now is the solution for Bavaria. What will be interesting now is what happens elsewhere."

Based on 1996 figures, Bayerische Hypo- und Vereinsbank AG will have combined assets of 743 billion marks ($415 billion), outranking Dresdner and not far off market leader Deutsche Bank AG, which had total assets of 886 billion in 1996.

Pending cartel office approval -- which analysts say should not be problematic -- the merged bank will start operations in October and is aiming to achieve one billion marks in savings over the next five years.

Bank shares in general surged on the Frankfurt bourse on Monday, bucking a downward trend. Hypo-Bank stock jumped as much as 25 percent to trade just under the 75-mark buy offer price at 73 marks, before settling back to 68.05 marks, still up 16 percent.
The news has brought to an end almost a year of speculation about how the Bavarian banks in particular are likely to face a more competitive future, but many questions remain unanswered.

The new bank will be far less diversified than the banks that hitherto formed the Big Three -- Deutsche, Dresdner and Commerzbank AG -- which could mean it will be on the lookout for acquisitions to boost its investment banking side, analysts said. The banks themselves said this was possible.
"Both these banks are weak in investment banking and two weaknesses will not create one strength," said Hein. "Something may have to be done here."

Moreover, the merger agreement leaves open the issue of expansion plans at Deutsche Bank, whose announcement last August that it had a 5.21 percent stake in Vereinsbank triggered a frenzy of merger rumours on the stock market.

Dresdner Bank's future is also an open issue, after the Bavarian agreement killed off talk that it would link up with Hypo-Bank. Dresdner and Hypo have in common the insurance giant Allianz as a major shareholder and strategic partner.

Finally, Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG could prove a wild card, after it moved last month to merge its primary insurance business with rival Victoria, creating an insurance group large enough to challenge Allianz.

Some analysts believe Munich Re could turn its attention to the banking sector, enabling it to compete better with Deutsche and Allianz, whose networks of crossholdings mean they can span a broad range of banking and insurance services.
"I think the takeover rumours can only continue now, especially for the smaller banks," said Commerzbank's Hein.

Matthew Czepliewicz, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers, cut Vereinsbank to a "hold" from "buy" on the news, noting that merger rumours have almost doubled its share price in the past year, but said the merger was nonetheless good news.
"We are pleased to see that the consolidation in the German banking sector has started sooner rather than later," he said.
Germany is regarded as heavily overbanked with more than 3,600 commercial, public and cooperative banks battling for market share, and a rate of one branch per 1,100 inhabitants.
But top bankers had consistently dismissed the prospect of an early outbreak of mergers among private-sector banks, saying the public banks would be the first to consolidate.

Political pressure is thought to have accelerated the move towards a Bavarian fusion. Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber is widely thought to have played a key role in securing the agreement between the two banks -- which will be viewed in Munich as a major coup for a financial centre that feels itself overshadowed by Frankfurt.
Salomon's Czepliewicz said the new bank's outlook could be clouded by political pressure to keep job cuts to a minimum.
"We are a little surprised by several aspects such as the limited scale of staff cuts indicated (5,000 to 7,000 according to industry sources)," Czepliewicz said,

"And I think the savings planned (one billion marks in five years) are a little optimistic based on that sort of staffing. I also think the plan to spread savings over five years could have been more aggressive," he added.
